    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his proposal for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    It has been revealed that fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    According to recent reports, “It’s totally phenomenal,” he remarked, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    According to recent reports, it was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    Industry observers note that rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he remarked. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and stated he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    Recent findings suggest that “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he stated. “Nobody got how major this was until it indicated up on their doorstep.”.

    Quilici noted he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy stated at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    In a recent development, “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most notable and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement noted.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    Sources indicate that “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” stated Kim Shirley.

    In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    Recent findings suggest that but when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and stated he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he mentioned, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

    Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa Group intends to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

    Sources indicate that the airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

    Tech giant leaders said their 2024 turnaround initiative, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

    “The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter said.

    Lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

    Sources indicate that lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

    According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

    Toxic Lufthansa Aims 1,000 Job Cuts But Cannot Explain Which Jobs Will Go

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs as management warns that its turnaround is falling short.
    • According to an internal letter to employees, Lufthansa management looks to cut approximately 1,000 full-time positions across its two main hubs.
    • The letter, signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and his fellow board members, describes an airline struggling to become competitive.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs as management warns that its turnaround is falling short. The financial problems are real, but I am skeptical that another vaguely defined job-cut announcement will help an airline that desperately needs to make peace with its employees in order to ultimately succeed.

    According to an internal letter to employees, Lufthansa management looks to cut approximately 1,000 full-time positions across its two main hubs.

    The letter, signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and his fellow board members, describes an airline struggling to become competitive. Management reported an adjusted operating loss of €180 million for the first nine months of 2026, an average of €20 million per month. It cited high fuel costs, the Middle East conflict, and nine strike days among the pressures on the business. Management also acknowledged shortcomings in costs, efficiency, and productivity.

    But several basic details remain unclear:.

    (That last point is particularly important).

    It has been revealed that the pilot union Vereinigung Cockpit responded sharply, accusing management of using an ominous but imprecise announcement to pressure employees as labor negotiations remain unresolved. The union wants answers about which jobs are affected and whether these are additional reductions. It also argues that management must take responsibility for its own operational and strategic decisions.

    Ground-staff union Verdi has raised similar concerns. Proposed savings include consolidating technical and administrative work at the moment performed separately within the organization. There may be a sensible case for that, but telling employees that 1,000 positions will disappear without explaining where or how is an excellent way to spread anxiety far beyond the people ultimately affected….

    I keep thinking about my Lufthansa A340-600 flight from Frankfurt to Washington earlier this year.

    Recent findings suggest that it was a superb flight, despite a business class seat that was well behind the competition. The improved food and bedding helped, but one of the main reasons I enjoyed it so much was the crew.

    The flight attendants were friendly and engaging: the flight attendant working my side was so pleasant. I also sensed pride in delivering the improved onboard service, even though the new service flow created more work.

    Those employees gave me a reason to look forward to flying Lufthansa again.

    Recent findings suggest that that anecdote certainly does not establish how many employees Lufthansa needs or whether its current labor agreements are sustainable (and this announcement does not suggest any crew positions are being cut). But my experience illustrates something management should remember as it tries to rebuild the business: good employees can make passengers want to come back, even when the seat itself is nothing special. And “happy employees make happy customers” include ground staff, lounge staff, and customer service folks too.

    According to recent reports, lufthansa has published its latest proposal to the pilot union, offering the prospect of up to 1,000 cockpit hires by 2033 and up to 150 additional captain promotions annually. In exchange, it seeks changes to compensation and productivity. The proposal also includes one-time payments for 2027 and 2028, with salary increases beginning in 2029.

    According to recent reports, those prospective hires are a separate issue from the proposed hub job cuts. The different figures concern different roles and timeframes.

    It has been revealed that management should not have to accept every union demand and employees also have an interest in a financially viable airline: reaching an agreement will require concessions. But Lufthansa must find a way to make peace with its workforce. The latest announcement has already inflamed matters, and I struggle to see how leaving so much uncertainty helps either side reach an agreement.

    If Lufthansa can eliminate unnecessary duplication while protecting the operation and treating affected employees fairly, it should be clear about it. I want Lufthansa to succeed. My A340 flight reminded me how good it can be. I would hate to see the enthusiasm I encountered onboard become another casualty of the never-ending conflict between management and labor.

    Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 full-time positions in Frankfurt and Munich, but has yet to publicly explain several essential details, including whether those reductions are part of an existing program.

    Cost control is necessary, especially as market uncertainty and high oil prices continue. But so is a workforce willing to help deliver the airline that Lufthansa wants passengers to pay a premium to fly. My recent experience demonstrated how much its employees contribute, and I hope management can find a path to profitability that gives those employees a reason to remain invested in its success. Lufthansa is in desperate need of strong leadership…I’ll just leave it at that.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    These days, retirement can come in many different forms—and arrive at many different ages. Some may choose to spend their golden years indulging in newly introduced hobbies, sports, and skills, while others may decide to focus on spending more quality time with family or take off and travel the world.

    It’s all about living life your way and celebrating your passions. But no matter when you choose to pull the career plug, everyone deserves to find a home base that can best support your newfound lifestyle. After all, not being tied down to an office or career means you can finally move to your dream city, or bop between your favorite travel destinations.

    Industry observers note that to help guide that decision, WalletHub has released its annual Best & Worst Places to Retire list—a ranking of 182 cities across the US (including the 150 most populated US cities, plus at least two of the most populated cities in each state) based on affordability, activities, quality of life, and healthcare. Unsurprisingly, four Florida cities made the Top 10—including claiming all top three spots—powered by the state's tax-free policies and warm weather.

    Here are the 10 best places to retire in the US, according to this year’s WalletHub study, along with supporting data we’ve pulled from the US Census Bureau, Zillow, city governments, and the demographic data firm Best Places. Whether you end up chasing sunshine or snowflakes, small towns or urban hubs, the words “retirement home” could be much more exciting than you think.

    This gallery has been updated with newly introduced information since its original publication date.

    With dramatic rivers and bridges dotting its scenery, and a culture and food scene that is constantly reinventing itself, Pittsburgh isn’t just a place to be—it’s a place to make home. Even with all the benefits of an urban hub, housing prices are generally lower than in most of the country. Pittsburgh is also known for having some of the best hospitals in the nation, with an array of social services designed to take care of senior residents. The list of activities to do here is endless, whether it’s taking the Duquesne or Monongahela inclines to see sky-high views of the river confluences, or exploring the latest exhibits at local museums like the Carnegie Museum of Art and Andy Warhol Museum, or the quirky Randyland. And of course, the food options here are diverse and delightful, from Italian neighborhood favorite DiAnoia’s Eatery to take-out from Lucy’s Banh Mi, lovingly made and served out of a makeshift trailer.

    Population: 302,971 (median age: 34.4 years).

    In a recent development, cost of living: The median home price is $234,620, over $130,000 less than the national median. Rent is also significantly lower, with the average being $1,550.

    Recent findings suggest that income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 160 sunny days per year; average lows of 21°F in winter; average highs of 84°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Pittsburgh has 38.1 physicians per 10,000 residents, above the US average.

    Honestly, could there be a better place to retire? Charleston is the best of every world, starting with a burgeoning culinary scene. Among the standouts are southern staples like Miller’s All Day and Callie’s Hot Little Biscuit, seafood spots like Leon’s Oyster Shop and Hank’s Seafood Restaurant, and modern favorites Chubby Fish, Frannie and the Fox, and Bar 167. Add to that a walkable downtown (including the local open-air market hall Charleston City Market) and waterfront (with the iconic Pineapple Fountain!).

    Population: 150,227 (median age: 36.6 years).

    Sources indicate that cost of living: The median home cost in Charleston is $587,511—about 1.6 the national median. The average rent is $3,000 (an increase of about $100 since last year).

    Income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 209 sunny days per year; average lows of 39°F in winter; average highs of 90°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Charleston has 47.8 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

    Industry observers note that while Fort Lauderdale may be best known for its beaches, the city’s appeal extends far beyond the coastline these days. With a plethora of waterfront condos to call home, days can be spent touring art galleries in Flagler Village, taking cooking classes at Sistrunk Market, or birding at Hugh Taylor Birch State Park and Secret Woods Nature Center. Plus, sports fans will love the roster of teams to cheer on, like soccer and hockey—and Miami Heat and Miami Dolphins’ home stadiums are both a short drive away.

    Population: 182,760 (median age: 42.5 years).

    Sources indicate that cost of living: The median home cost in Fort Lauderdale is $509,743—a slight drop from last year, but still much higher than the national median. The average rent is $2,700 (an increase of about $100 since last year).

    In a recent development, income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 246 sunny days per year; average lows of 59°F in winter; average highs of 90°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Fort Lauderdale has 22.4 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

    As long as you can tolerate some mightily cold winters, retiring in Minneapolis means you’re never far from great independent retailers, worthwhile museums, scenic lakes, and dining experiences that extend far beyond the tater tot hotdish. Despite falling four rankings from last year, the City of Lakes still has plenty going for it. The best part? “Minnesota nice” is a very real thing, so there’s a pretty good chance you’ll end up with a friendly neighbor.

    Population: 429,954 (median age: 33.3 years).

    Cost of living: The median home cost in Minneapolis is $328,351, which is lower than the national median. The average rent is a reasonable $1,717.

    Income tax on social security? Yes.

    Climate: 198 sunny days per year; average lows of 7°F in winter; average highs of 84°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Minneapolis has 33.9 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

    Atlanta is chock full of activities, be it museums, sports, live music, or just getting outside and taking it all in. All that and more contributes to the Georgia capital ranking 4 out of 170 in Wallethub’s activities index. One new attraction is the Atlanta Beltline, a greenway that's currently being built around the city, which debuted its Southside and Southeast trails this year. Travel lovers will also appreciate being near Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport—the busiest international airport in the world. And don’t forget to mix in the city’s innovative Southern food scene, with diverse highlights like Mary Mac’s Tea Room, Rina, and Botiwalla by Chai Pani.

    Population: 498,715 (median age: 34.5 years).

    Cost of living: The median home cost in Atlanta is $380,331, which is higher than the national median. The average rent is $2,089, above the national average.

    Income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 217 sunny days per year; average lows of 33°F in winter; average highs of 88°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Atlanta has 36.5 physicians per 10,000 residents (above the national average).

    Industry observers note that if city life isn’t quite how you imagined spending your golden years, Casper, Wyoming, is perfect for those seeking a Ron Swanson-style retirement. Spend your days fly-fishing, canoeing, and hiking right outside your door—not to mention day-trip access to Grand Teton and Rocky Mountain national parks. In terms of culture, there are plenty of art museums, planetariums, and historic sites to continue that sense of exploration. As an added bonus, it’s by far one of the least expensive towns on this list—WalletHub ranked it 3rd out of 182 for affordability. It’s no wonder it leaped five spots from last year up to fifth place.

    Population: 59,038 (median age: 37.3 years).

    Cost of living: The median home sale price in Casper is $310,650, which is lower than the national median. The average rent is $1,350, up $150 from last year.

    It has been revealed that income tax on social security? No.

    Healthcare: Casper has 19.7 physicians per 10,000 residents (a bit below the national average).

    As the No. 1 city in WalletHub's quality of life metric, Scottsdale is easily one of the best places to retire in the US, despite sinking two spots from last year. It is a famously popular spot for golfers, but it also boasts plenty of destination spas, incredible art and architecture, and James Beard Award-winning restaurants to satisfy retirees of all types. Another upside: 330 sunny days a year. Just be prepared for really, really hot summers—average temperatures from June to September are all in the triple digits.

    Population: 241,361 (median age: 53 years).

    Income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 330 sunny days per year; average lows of 42°F in winter; average highs of 104°F in summer.

    Healthcare: Scottsdale has 20.1 physicians per 10,000 residents (below the national average).

    Industry observers note that tampa, on Florida's Gulf Coast, rose two spots to capture the bronze medal this year. The city itself has plenty of housing options, a buzzing Riverwalk, and one of the best airports in the country. With plenty of surrounding suburbs, it also makes a great jumping-off point for exploring other beach towns in the state. Foodies should take note, as Tampa is known for its restaurants—Rooster & the Till (run by James Beard semi-finalist Ferrell Alvarez) and 384,959 (median age: 36.3 years) (beloved for its Cuban sandwiches) are two stand-outs.

    Population: 384,959 (median age: 36.3 years).

    Cost of living: The median home cost in Tampa is $375,619, up just 0.4 percent over last year. The average rent is $1,962/month, down $95 since last year.

    It has been revealed that income tax on social security? No.

    Climate: 246 sunny days per year; average lows of 52°F in winter; average highs of 90°F in summer.

    According to recent reports, miami rose two spots since last year to the runner-up position. It may not be quite as affordable as other cities, but Miami has enough art galleries, Cuban food, golf courses, beaches, and museums to justify the rent. (And who wouldn’t love the chance to drive down to Key West whenever they want?) Miami-Dade County even offers an “Active Older Adults Program” that provides free fitness classes, games, field trips and arts activities for people ages 55 and older. Plus it ranks the sixth most walkable city on this list, with most residents having access to public transportation within walking distance of their homes.

    Population: 442,241 (median age: 41.2 years).

    Sources indicate that income tax on social security? No.

    For the third year in a row, Orlando snagged the trophy for the most retiree-friendly city in the nation. We’ve already mentioned the warm weather and low taxes of Florida, but Orlando has a particular abundance of quiet communities, great restaurants, and independent stores—and its inland location means you won’t have to worry quite as much during hurricane season. (Bonus: Given Orlando’s proximity to theme parks, it’ll be easy to convince family to visit, too.).

    Population: 307,573 (median age: 35.4 years).

    Industry observers note that this was a late evening flight where I had planned to eat in the lounge before my flight but due to a flight delay jumped onto an earlier flight. It was 8:00 pm, I had not eaten, and had I been flying on United I would have been out of luck since you have to pre-order any food onboard beyond snack boxes.

    I figured I would have to make a Taco Bell run in LA when I landed, but this proved enough..and my body thanks me.

    American Airlines has a very good buy-on-board cheese plate. I enjoyed all three cheeses, the crackers were excellent, the apples were sweet, and the Toblerone was a nice dessert.

    Simple food can be very satisfying when the ingredients are good. This is something American does better than Delta or United in economy class, and I would gladly order it again.

    p.s. If you’re still feeling peckish, you might also enjoy a bag of salted, mixed nuts from Nuts & Clark…$11 or 1,100 miles. Also recommended!

    #168533. Traveling This Thanksgiving? Here’s the Latest on Flight Delays Following Delta Outage

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1448 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Traveling This Thanksgiving? Here’s the Latest on Flight Delays Following Delta Outage

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Sunday, November 22, US travelers faced another wave of significant flight disruptions ahead of Thanksgiving.
    • This time around, the issues occurred at the nation’s busiest hub, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL), where Delta Air Lines delayed hundreds of flights due to a problem with a critical piece of technology.
    • The delays sent ripple effects throughout the carrier's US network, snarling travel looks for thousands of Delta fliers heading out on Thanksgiving trips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Sunday, November 22, US travelers faced another wave of significant flight disruptions ahead of Thanksgiving.

    This time around, the issues occurred at the nation’s busiest hub, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL), where Delta Air Lines delayed hundreds of flights due to a problem with a critical piece of technology.

    The delays sent ripple effects throughout the carrier's US network, snarling travel looks for thousands of Delta fliers heading out on Thanksgiving trips. While the concern was resolved Sunday afternoon, the airline delayed 300 flights and canceled 92 flights on Monday morning, according to FlightAware. “Operations are stable today with automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations fully restored,” a Delta spokesperson told Traveler on Monday. “Delta teams are focused on keeping the operation moving safely and caring for our customers.”.

    For US travelers, the timing is particularly stressful. AAA projects 5.96 million travelers will take domestic flights over the Thanksgiving holiday period. Plus, Delta’s operational difficulties came only nine days after the FAA declared a rare nationwide ground stop on November 13 that lasted more than four hours and led to multiple days of travel chaos.

    It has been revealed that while Delta’s technology issues had nothing to do with the FAA systems, both incidents have travelers questioning if their Thanksgiving travel plans will be disrupted. Here’s a look at the current situation and what travelers should know before heading to the airport this week.

    This article has been updated with newly introduced information since its original publish date.

    It has been revealed that on Sunday morning, Delta began having problems with its weight and balance automation system at the Atlanta airport. The system’s critical equipment assesses whether aircraft are too heavy to fly before takeoff.

    While the system was out, Delta crews use manual backup processes to help flights depart. However, the technology outage still led to thousands of delays and hundreds of cancellations.

    In a recent development, delta had 2,194 flight delays on November 22, which is about 64% of its schedule, according to FlightAware data. The carrier also had 274 canceled flights on Sunday. Although some of those disruptions were due to other challenges, like bad weather in the Northeast, Delta stated that 70% of the flight changes were caused by the ATL equipment problems, according to CNN.

    It has been revealed that the airline stated it had restored the system by Sunday afternoon. By Monday morning, Delta’s flight schedules across the country appeared to be getting back on track. However, as of 11 a.m. ET on Monday, the carrier had accumulated more than 300 flight delays and 92 cancellations, FlightAware demonstrated. Now that the technology issue has been resolved, travelers can expect Delta's flight schedule to progressively return to normal but should still prepare for lingering delays through Tuesday, November 24.

    Industry observers note that travelers with canceled flights can ask for a full cash refund if they no longer wish to travel. The carrier doesn’t charge passengers to change their flights if they’re booked in any fare class except basic economy (although a difference in fare may apply).

    Industry observers note that passengers should continue to check with Delta for the latest information on their flight status. When traveling for Thanksgiving, err on the side of caution and plan to arrive at the airport early: at least two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international one.

    The ground stop on November 13 was due to a separate concern with air traffic control equipment outages and the telecommunications systems that the FAA uses to track and communicate with planes while they’re flying. “The ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution,” notes the FAA’s statement. “Safety is, and will always remain, the FAA’s highest priority. We will never compromise the safety of the flying public.”.

    On November 13, the FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was updating telecommunications equipment at an FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the issues began, according to the FAA. The manufacturer was deploying a new router that also began to cause system disruptions at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. “The FAA’s legacy equipment became unstable when data began flooding the FAA FTI network, at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” claims an FAA statement. “This disrupted the system and created instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds.”.

    It has been revealed that once the inconsistencies were identified, the FAA claims that L3Harris blocked those two locations, and the network stabilized. However, the exact cause of the telecommunications problems are still under investigation.

    Regulators are still working to identify the root cause of the glitch. “The work that was done on Friday, that's been done thousands of times by L3Harris in our network,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a recent interview on ABC’s “This Week.” “It's been done thousands of times by other companies, and these problems haven't arisen, and so that's why we have to figure out what went wrong here.”.

    Duffy also noted that the equipment in question is several decades old: the router was originally purchased in 2001 and was also part of a system that ran on obsolete copper wiring.

    Experts say that the archaic equipment underscores the urgent need to update the nation’s air traffic control system. “While the investigation continues, the incident exposed a troubling reality: America's aviation system remains vulnerable because we have relied on aging infrastructure for far too long,” says Geoff Freeman, president and CEO of US Travel Association. The “disruption was a wake-up call that Washington cannot afford to ignore.”.

    For many US airlines, the busy Thanksgiving travel season began with early departures on November 19 and is expected to last through December 1.

    Air travel experts say that the FAA ground stop’s effects on Thanksgiving travel plans should be minimal. As of November 16, the majority of airline flight schedules were back on track. Delta was also able to restore its systems on Sunday, November 22; as of Monday, flight schedules began returning to normal but Delta fliers could still encounter lingering delays early this week.

    It has been revealed that it helps that fewer travelers are expected to fly this Thanksgiving compared to recent years. According to Mike Arnot, spokesman for Cirium, an aviation analytics company, the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is usually one of the busiest air travel days of the year. But in 2026, it’s not even slated to be in the top 50 busiest days for flying.

    Travelers should still continue to check with their airline for the latest travel updates and plan to be at the airport at least two hours before takeoff for a domestic flight.

    Operations are largely back on track, so many airlines have ended the flexible rebooking waivers that were issued at the beginning of the ground stop.

    Recent findings suggest that however, Delta is still allowing passengers who were scheduled to fly through Monday, November 16 to make changes to their flights at no extra cost through November 23. Customers' fresh departure dates must be on or before November 23, according to the airline’s rebooking policy.

    Sources indicate that even if your airline no longer has a travel waiver in place, if you’re flying with a major US carrier, you likely have the ability to change your flight without paying a fee (although a difference in fare may apply). However, these policies usually do not apply to low-cost carriers or tickets booked in basic economy class.

    Industry observers note that it’s impossible to predict if a nationwide ground stop could happen again, according to Freeman of the US Travel Association. However, modernizing the air traffic control system should reduce these types of outages in the long run.

    Recent findings suggest that “The FAA is making progress, replacing outdated copper communications lines with high-speed fiber, upgrading radar and radio systems, and introducing technology that allows air traffic controllers to manage flights more efficiently,” Freeman indicates. “For travelers, these investments should mean fewer delays, more reliable flights, and greater confidence that the system can handle disruptions.”.

    Sources indicate that airline executives echoed a similar sentiment regarding the state of US air traffic control systems. “This moment must be a call to action,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement emailed to media. “It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now.”.

    Following the ground stop, the DOT requested an additional $50.1 billion from Congress to complete its overhaul of the national air traffic control system.

    For more information on passenger rights during airline technology outages, read our full guide.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Mother Claims Delta Seated Her Toddler Separately And Told Her To Ask Other Passengers To Move

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A mother states Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats.
    • Recent findings suggest that in a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL).
    • She says she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A mother states Delta Air Lines separated her from her two-year-old daughter, then told her to ask other passengers to switch seats. She says she had purchased Comfort+ and originally selected seats together. If her account is accurate, this was a problem for Delta to resolve before boarding, not something to leave a parent negotiating in the aisle.

    Recent findings suggest that in a Reddit post, a passenger describes trying to resolve separate seat assignments on a flight from Orlando (MCO) to Atlanta (ATL). She was traveling with her husband, their 2½-year-old daughter, and their one-year-old son.

    She says she was directed to the gate for assistance, but received this response:.

    In a recent development, “I explained that she’s two and cannot sit by herself. Their solution? Tell me it was my responsibility to ask other passengers to switch seats.”.

    Recent findings suggest that when commenters questioned whether she had purchased basic economy or failed to select seats, she clarified that she had booked Comfort+. After checking her original confirmation, she added:.

    Sources indicate that “I just looked and it was definitely Delta. I have 3 flight / time changes – I originally booked us in 15 D / 15 E / 15 F – we ended up in 15 F / 15 A / 16 A.”.

    This remains her account and we don’t have a way to verify the booking history or the exchange with the gate staff. She also does not clearly state how the family ultimately sat onboard.

    I have traveled extensively with my children, including when they were very young. There is a considerable difference between wanting the entire family together and needing a two-year-old beside a parent.

    It is unreasonable to ask an airline to rearrange a cabin so that every adult in a traveling party can sit together. Heidi and I can sit apart. One parent can sit with one child while the other sits elsewhere with the other child. We have done that many times.

    Sources indicate that but a toddler needs an adult who can help with the seatbelt, food, and everything else that comes with flying at that age. The stranger assigned to the adjacent seat cannot reasonably become the person expected to provide that help.

    I see no excuse for the Delta agent. Once an agent knows a toddler has been assigned a seat away from both parents, someone needs to take responsibility for finding a workable arrangement and it should be someone in a position of authority…like the gate agent.

    I am also sympathetic to passengers who pre-select a seat and then find themselves pressured to move.

    It has been revealed that A parent should not board, occupy someone else’s seat, and announce that the family needs to sit together and a passenger should not be shamed for declining an aisle-to-middle swap. There may be very good reasons that person selected that particular seat, and those reasons are not necessarily anyone else’s business.

    That is precisely why the airline should handle this.

    It has been revealed that an agent can review the seat map, identify possible swaps, and ask for volunteers. If necessary, the airline can offer an incentive rather than expect a stranger to absorb the inconvenience for free. There may also be a solution involving a different cabin, provided the family agrees and any fare difference is addressed.

    Industry observers note that the ultimate solution to situations like these does not have to preserve every preference the family had when booking. It does need to put a young child beside a responsible adult.

    The published Delta family seating policy states:.

    “Delta strives to seat family members together upon request.”.

    Sources indicate that it directs customers who cannot obtain seats together online or through the app to contact reservations to review the available options. That wording is less reassuring than a guarantee. Even so, I would expect the assistance to amount to more than telling a parent to start asking around once onboard.

    Parents should understand fare restrictions and select seats when possible, but a two-year-old’s need to sit beside a parent does not disappear because the family purchased a cheaper ticket and it becomes legally dicey to not sell basic economy tickets to young children. However, in this case it was not a basic economy ticket but a Comfort+ seat.

    Recent findings suggest that selecting seats months in advance does not mean you can stop checking them. Whenever I receive a schedule change, I review the flights and seat assignments and check again often in the week leading up to travel. Be sure to take a screenshot of your original seat assignments if they were not reflected on your ticket confirmation.

    If a young child becomes separated from a parent, contact the airline promptly and explain the child’s age. If reservations cannot resolve it, arrive early and ask an airport agent…don’t agree to negotiate onboard…it’s unreasonable, even for Frontier Airlines.

    This is called “gardening” your reservation.

    A mother says Delta assigned her toddler a separate seat and left her to ask other passengers to move, despite originally booking seats together in Comfort+. We have only her account, but the underlying expectation is reasonable: a two-year-old should sit beside a parent, and the airline should help arrange that.

    Other passengers deserve respect for their seat choices too. Resolving the glitch before boarding protects everyone from an awkward confrontation that should never have been necessary….

    • Recent findings suggest that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    Recent findings suggest that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    It has been revealed that advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly remarked it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

    According to recent reports, senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump stated, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    Industry observers note that “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most key stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations mentioned. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    It has been revealed that the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

    “Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After a three-year hiatus, American Airlines is preparing to resume service to Israel.

    According to recent reports, the carrier stated Friday that it will restart flights from Newly introduced York-JFK to Tel Aviv on March 27, 2027. Flights will operate daily using Boeing 777-200ER aircraft.

    According to recent reports, american has not flown to Israel since the Hamas attack on southern Israel in October 2023. It remained on the sidelines even as rivals United and Delta resumed service to Ben Gurion International Airport, though they too were forced to temporarily pause flights during fighting between Israel and Iran.

    Sources indicate that israeli officials had questioned why American was slow to reconnect the country, citing the importance of air links between Tel Aviv and New York. The airline did not offer an explanation beyond concern for the safety of its passengers and crew.

    Sources indicate that american also said Friday that it has formed a commercial partnership with Tel Aviv-based low-cost carrier Israir. The agreement will expand in phases over time, American said; in the first phase, Israir will place its code on American’s flights between JFK and Tel Aviv.

    The carriers will also work to implement an interline agreement that would give Israir customers access to American’s network across the U.S., Canada, Latin America, and the Caribbean from JFK.

    Recent findings suggest that “American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire,” American Senior Vice President of Alliances Anmol Bhargava stated in a news release. “As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”.

    Recent findings suggest that israir operates five weekly flights between JFK and Tel Aviv using Airbus A330-200 aircraft. Fresh York is its only U.S. destination; most of its network is concentrated in the Near East and Europe.

    Airline Elite Status So Close, Yet So Far: The Drawback To Being A Free Agent

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that I boast often about being a free agent when it comes to both hotels and airlines…I’m done chasing elite status (at least top-tier elite status) because the cost/benefit analysis no longer works for me.
    • I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement.
    • And sometimes after another great United flight, like my journey back to California over the weekend, I do wonder if I  am better served just getting back on the hamster wheel and putting most of my eggs in the United basket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that I boast often about being a free agent when it comes to both hotels and airlines…I’m done chasing elite status (at least top-tier elite status) because the cost/benefit analysis no longer works for me. But there are some days I wonder….

    I fly United quite a bit and if I’m being honest, the experience is usually excellent…I seek out the A321neo, as Starlink has shifted from a nice bonus to requirement. But it’s not just that. The food has improved and service has been great..flight attendants appear happy (they have a contract after all) and the operation has also been good: my personal on-time arrival rate with United is over 90% while it hovers at around 50% for American.

    And sometimes after another great United flight, like my journey back to California over the weekend, I do wonder if I  am better served just getting back on the hamster wheel and putting most of my eggs in the United basket. This flight was from Chicago to Los Angeles and I just missed the upgrade to first class as a Gold…had I been Platinum, I would have scored an upgrade.

    In a recent development, I’m close…not that I’m projected to spend $5K in the last month of the year on United airfare…but it is conceivably within reach. And in the next month I’m flying Aer Lingus, American, Delta, JetBlue, KLM, and United….maybe even more.

    And having Premier Platinum status would certainly help with some upgrades and I’d put the PlusPoints to use….

    But then I pinch myself and think I’m actually only 2/3 there with 1/12 of the year left…and to spend all that money on United instead of flying the carriers and routings and times that work best for me (mostly in premium cabins…) just doesn’t make sense.

    So I return to reality and think, no, the status just isn’t worth it and if I really need the premium cabin seat, I’ll pay for it. And the irony is that the majority of my flights this year have been in premium cabins and to reach top-tier status you have to essentially buy premium cabin fares anyway or else you will never spend enough. So what’s the point? Free baggage? Extra legroom seats for the family? I don’t find that worthwhile.

    So I guess the bottom line is that by splitting my loyalty this year I’ll make Gold on American and Gold on United (nothing on Alaska, Delta, or JetBlue, though I have flown them all) whereas I could have rather easily made Platinum on United had I been a bit more loyal to a product that I do genuinely like.

    But no. I still think I’m making the correct choice for my circumstances.

    And yet it’s the allure of frequent flyer elite status is still somewhat enchanting….

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    While I love staying at a really great five-star hotel, there is a time and place for renting an Airbnb. For me, it's when I'm vacationing in the Caribbean. On my most recent trip to the area, I holed up in a sprawling Puerto Rico villa with a path to the beach and a private pool overlooking the sea. My family and I spent most of our time barefoot, and there was room for everyone to spread out before gathering in the kitchen to whip up dinner. It’s one of my favorite memories—and one anyone can replicate almost anywhere in the Caribbean.

    From coral stone houses in Barbados to beach cottages in the Bahamas and stays in St. Barts with incredible sea views, the properties across this region have their own distinct rhythm. Whether you’re looking for a chic modern condo in a vibrant port town or an overwater villa where you can dive straight into the sea, the options are as diverse as the islands themselves. And trust me, there’s something special about having a little taste of the tropics all to yourself. If you're ready to book a trip of your own, read on for my favorite Airbnbs across the Caribbean.

This four-bedroom villa shoulders the mile-long Shoal Bay Beach, but that’s hardly its only selling point. Groups also flock here for its primo chef’s kitchen (complete with a professional gas range stove), formal indoor dining room and casual alfresco seating situation, tiled outdoor hot tub, and private swimming pool. Need a hand in planning your daily excursions? The property manager is happy to assist with car rentals, ferry and taxi reservations, hiring a nanny, or arranging water sports.

    Location: Shoal Bay Village, AnguillaThings to do nearby: Shoal Bay East, beach restaurants, The Valley excursions.

    How many countries are in the Caribbean?

    It has been revealed that the Caribbean is a diverse region made up of over 700 islands, islets, reefs, and cays, but not all are independent countries. In total, there are 13 sovereign nations and 17 dependent territories spread across the Caribbean Sea. The independent countries include popular destinations such as Jamaica, the Bahamas, Barbados, St. Lucia, and Trinidad and Tobago. The dependent territories—like Puerto Rico (US), Martinique (France), and the Cayman Islands (UK)—offer a mix of cultural influences and governance structures. While each island varies in size, language, and history, the entire region is united by its tropical climate, vibrant cultures, and rich mix of African, European, and Indigenous heritage.

    What is the best island to visit in the Caribbean?

    There isn’t one “best” Caribbean island—it just depends on what kind of experience you’re seeking. Families often love Jamaica for its all-inclusive resorts, kid-friendly activities, and easy flights from the US. Surfers gravitate toward Barbados and Puerto Rico, which boast consistent swells and a laid-back surf culture. Solo travelers often choose Puerto Rico or Curaçao, thanks to their safety, walkable cities, and friendly locals. For romantic getaways, St. Lucia and Antigua are top picks—think private villas, lush rainforests, and stunning beaches perfect for couples. And for multi-generational trips, the Bahamas or Turks and Caicos stand out, offering luxury accommodations, calm beaches for kids, and plenty of excursions for all ages. Each island has its own rhythm and charm, so the “best” one depends on your travel style and interests.

    When is the best time to travel to the Caribbean?

    Industry observers note that the best time to visit the Caribbean typically falls between December and April, during the region’s dry season. This period offers warm temperatures, low humidity, and minimal rainfall—ideal conditions for beach days and outdoor adventures. However, it’s also the peak tourist season, meaning higher prices and more crowds. For travelers seeking better deals and fewer tourists, the shoulder months of May, June, and November are excellent alternatives, offering good weather with occasional rain showers. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November, and while severe storms are rare on most islands, it’s wise to stay informed about forecasts if traveling during this time.

    Which islands in the Caribbean are the most affordable?

    Jamaica and the Dominican Republic are good places to start if you're looking for budget-friendly rentals. But keep in mind that no matter which island you head to, the neighborhood and season you're traveling in matter just as much as anything else, and an exclusive beachfront address can promptly change your budget. To get the most bang for your buck, consider traveling during shoulder or off seasons, and take a look at rentals outside of the typical tourist hot spots.

    Are there any islands in the Caribbean you can visit from the US without a passport?

    Industry observers note that yes. US citizens traveling directly from the mainland can visit Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands without a passport. The US Virgin Islands include St. Thomas, St. John, and St. Croix, and travelers can also head to Puerto Rico’s offshore islands of Vieques and Culebra.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    Sources indicate that seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.

    In a recent development, seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    Sources indicate that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    American will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A new reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

    Recent findings suggest that “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle declared in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.
    • Recent findings suggest that budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.

    Recent findings suggest that budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    “I think it’s outrageous,” remarked Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking key.”.

    Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he mentioned on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    In a recent development, johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

    Industry observers note that there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson stated Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    It has been revealed that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    Industry observers note that A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a blueprint in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle remarked they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability concern, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” noted Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

    The Essential Cookbooks to Break Out Every Holiday Season

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the holidays always bring about a flurry of travel, but even if you find yourself hosting in your own home this year, you can always explore new frontiers by way of a good cookbook.
    • We'd love to hear about the cookbooks that take a place of pride in your kitchen on Instagram or Facebook.
    • It has been revealed that I was lucky enough to taste chef Ifrah Ahmed's food at a beautiful dinner last year, so I couldn't wait to add her cookbook Soomaaliya to my shelf when it came out this spring.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the holidays always bring about a flurry of travel, but even if you find yourself hosting in your own home this year, you can always explore new frontiers by way of a good cookbook. At Traveler, the titles we swear by take us through H Mart with an expert guide at hand to break down the aisles, to Sri Lanka, where the palette of London hot spot Hoppers was formed, and to the sugar-dusted counters of Broma Bakery, where Sarah Fennel has the key to 100 desserts sure to satisfy any sweet tooth. The best cookbooks immerse you in the corner of the world they come from, and through their pages, narrative transforms into a multi-sensory experience. Just as we're placing finishing touches on our holiday menus, our editors gathered their favorite cookbooks of all time that take readers all across the map, from recent releases that have become instant classics in our households to vintage volumes that continue to stand the test of time.

    We'd love to hear about the cookbooks that take a place of pride in your kitchen on Instagram or Facebook.

    It has been revealed that I was lucky enough to taste chef Ifrah Ahmed's food at a beautiful dinner last year, so I couldn't wait to add her cookbook Soomaaliya to my shelf when it came out this spring. In Somalia, she writes, "knowledge is passed down orally," but she records the flavors and traditions of the culture in this stunning homage to Somalia's rich culinary legacy. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

    When I’m working my way through a recipe or just slapping something together for the sake of a pantry clean-out, odds are that the secret ingredient that ties it all together is an item I picked up at H Mart. Perhaps it’s the splash of Shaoxing cooking wine that makes all the notes in a fried rice sing that much more, or the half-packet of Buldak sauce that brings on the much-needed heat to some peanut noodles. As a card-carrying fan of the brand, I was ecstatic when I learned H Mart co-president Stacey Kwon had committed the splendor of the Korean grocery store’s aisles to pages in a cookbook. Beyond just housing recipes (the Galbi Jjim is a dinner party show-stopper), this omnibus also lets readers in on the store’s history, the tips and tricks of navigating its inventory, and handy guides that will have you cooking like it's second nature. This volume is a boon for H Mart enthusiasts and a fantastic tool for those just beginning their journey in the kitchen. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations.

    I love Hoppers, the dish. I love Hoppers, the homey London restaurant chain dishing out delicious Sri Lankan and southern Indian fare. So it’s a no-brainer that I love cooking from Hoppers, the cookbook. With the recipes in this book, author and restaurant owner Karan Gokani attempts to make traditional dishes like lamb kari and buriani feel approachable, all with the trademark come-join-me affability of his Instagram cooking videos. Some of these recipes are Proustian madeleines, taking me back to early-morning visits to fish markets in southern India or the many holidays spent along Sri Lanka’s southern coast, as well as to my grandmother’s dining table in Kerala. There’s a striking overlap in ingredients and flavors when it comes to Kerala and Sri Lanka, and it’s always a pleasure to get to sample that shared heritage. Now, if only I could summon a supply of the Arrack Attack cocktails from Hoppers as I cooked… —Arati Menon, global digital director.

    Recent findings suggest that since I’ve moved to Latest York, I’ve known that whenever I’m looking for a taste of home, I can always head to the East Village or Williamsburg to Taiwanese-American restaurant Win Son (and its bakery off-shoots). And now with the restaurant’s cookbook, I can recreate their lu rou fan (braised pork rice) or tsang ying tou (fly’s head, a fragrant mix of pork and chives that goes over rice) for myself. I’m fortunate to have grown up with a mom who was a fantastic cook, but the magic she worked in the kitchen has always been obscure to me. She’s true to the trope of never writing any recipes down, instead relying on muscle memory and years of road-tested intuition. But with the wisdom of Ku, Brown, and Erway’s book by my side, I’ve finally been able to master my childhood dishes and resist the urge to order takeout. —K.C.

    Recent findings suggest that I became interested in plant-based dining once I started dating a vegan, and one of the first restaurants that opened my eyes to all the possibilities of letting go of meat was Amanda Cohen’s Dirt Candy. It’s one of my favorite restaurants in the whole city, with a seasonal tasting menu that doesn’t break the bank but still stretches your imagination by showing you the full flavor spectrum of a leek, or proving by example that yes, eggplant really does belong in a dessert. Their cookbook is an absolute joy to read through, especially since it’s part comic book! It’s as fun as it is revelatory, and it’s a showcase of how cooking is an art as well as a form of play. —K.C.

    It has been revealed that A friend gifted me Table for Two when my partner and I moved in together a few years ago. It was sweet, and the cover added some much-needed color and beauty to my kitchen counter. But its not just a pretty face—this cookbook has challenged me. From slow-cooked lamb and cinnamon stew to fluffy, peach crepes, these recipes are made to impress. You’ll find a mix of one-pan meals, specialty dinners, delicious lunches, and rich desserts. If you’re trying to win someone over, this cookbook will help you every step of the way. —M.K.

    Industry observers note that when it comes to educational heroes, Alton Brown is on the pediment alongside Bill Nye and LeVar Burton for me. Watching his show Good Eats on Food Network was a formative ritual; he just has this infectious geekiness about him. As a sort of food mad scientist, Brown can be technical bordering on obsessive, but it’s that attention to detail that makes his methods so approachable: cooking is something you can break down to its basics and understand. This first volume is all about the fundamentals, and with it you’ll never make a bad batch of brownies or dry turkey again. —K.C.

    Sources indicate that I stumbled upon this vintage cookbook at a secondhand bookstore, and I initially purchased it as a novelty item. I’d never seen a cookbook dedicated to an appliance before, let alone one I had never associated with “cooking” to begin with. But much like how I’d imagine Methven’s initial readership reacted in 1978, I was pleasantly shocked and excited by how versatile the microwave really is. There are recipes ranging from Scallops Au Gratin to Barbecue Ribs to Seven-Minute Brownies in this book, and I’ve gleaned many staples from its pages. It’s only right to acknowledge you’re not going to get restaurant-quality versions or true-to-form authenticity out of every dish, but if you’re wiling to adventure, this is one of the most accessible ways to do it from your own home. Sometimes when I’m at a loss for what to make and feeling sluggish, I’ll perform a little bibliomancy on this book to figure out lunch. Even if you’re just interested in this title for your coffee table, the photography is beautiful and occasionally experimental in its efforts to display the science behind the latest-fangled microwave. —K.C.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view.
    • In the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014.
    • Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    As we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view. The question is not whether Republicans can recover from this, but whether the American system of government will be changed irreparably before they do. To what will Republicans return?

    In the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014. With 56 senators, it’s the Democrats’ biggest majority since 2009–10, when they peaked at 60 seats. Republicans haven’t had that many Senate seats since 1922, when the caucus was 59 seats after the 1920 landslide that repudiated Woodrow Wilson’s progressivism and swept Warren Harding into office. If you’re wondering, the largest-ever Republican Senate caucus, in absolute numbers rather than as a share of the chamber, was 60 in 1907; the largest Democratic caucus was 75 seats at the peak of the New Deal in 1937. There’s a reason why Franklin D. Roosevelt thought he could get away with Court-packing with 75 senators.

    Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    On “The Real Stakes of the Wilderness Years”.
