    How Much It Costs Emirates To Keep Its Airbus A380 Fleet Flying In 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that emirates is pouring billions of dollars into cabin overhauls and spending tens of thousands of dollars an hour on fuel and maintenance for an Airbus A380 fleet that other airlines are retiring early.
    • Industry observers note that at the center of that commitment is Emirates President Tim Clark, whose bet on the A380 stretches well into the next decade even as replacement aircraft deliveries slip and fuel markets stay volatile.
    • Industry estimates based on 2026 figures, place total A380 operating costs between $40,000 and $55,000 per flight hour, depending on fuel prices and mission length.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that emirates is pouring billions of dollars into cabin overhauls and spending tens of thousands of dollars an hour on fuel and maintenance for an Airbus A380 fleet that other airlines are retiring early. The carrier does not disclose what it spends to keep each superjumbo flying, so the true price tag of sustaining the world's largest passenger airliner is still hidden behind industry estimates, unscheduled technical directives, and a sprawling refurbishment program.

    Industry observers note that at the center of that commitment is Emirates President Tim Clark, whose bet on the A380 stretches well into the next decade even as replacement aircraft deliveries slip and fuel markets stay volatile. How much does keeping the A380 fleet flying in 2026 actually cost Emirates, and what keeps the airline paying the bill?

    Industry estimates based on 2026 figures, place total A380 operating costs between $40,000 and $55,000 per flight hour, depending on fuel prices and mission length. According to Golden Epaulets Aviation, fuel accounts for $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour; airport and navigation fees run $5,000 to $9,000; maintenance and engineering reach $8,000 to $12,000; and crew adds $4,000 to $6,000.

    In a recent development, fuel assumptions across aviation analyses vary sharply, showing how sensitive hourly burn is to crude and jet fuel pricing. While Golden Epaulets Aviation puts A380 fuel burn at $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour in 2026, estimates put it at $11,500 per hour, and energy markets have faced upward pressure since the Iran conflict began in 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that for the A380, engineering and maintenance bring a massive penalty that twin-engine widebodies avoid. Separate industry estimates put A380 maintenance alone at $6,000 to $8,000 per flight hour, reflecting the extra inspections, parts, and shop visits required across four engines rather than just two.

    Emirates is committing $5 billion to overhaul the cabin interiors of 219 aircraft, which, when broken down, comprise 110 A380s and 109 777s. It is natural to see such a move as pointless with latest-generation aircraft on the way, but delays to these new aircraft deliveries have led the airline to refresh existing widebodies, because retiring them is no longer a viable option. Originally scoped to cover 67 A380s and 53 777s, the program expanded in May 2024 by adding 43 more A380s and 28 more 777s as replacement jet timelines stretched out.

    Each A380 refurbishment comes with roughly 33,000 work hours over 21 days and more than 4,000 fresh parts, according to AeroTime. Across 44 months of work through April 2026, Emirates had completed 100 aircraft, 47 A380s and 53 777s, using 4.4 million work hours, with more than half of the 219-aircraft total projected to finish by December 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that in May, Emirates completed its first retrofit of a two-class A380, and a subsequent phase covering 60 A380s and 51 Boeing 777s began in August. When all is done, Emirates will be left with a fully refreshed fleet that meets the high demands of its most loyal customers, but keeping so many cabins out of line for three-week overhauls makes this cabin modernization a multi-year capital and hangar balancing act for the carrier.

    Industry observers note that of course, there are the scheduled checks and routine hourly burn, but unexpected technical mandates added sharp, unbudgeted costs to operating the A380. In October, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered turbine seal replacements on certain Engine Alliance GP7200 engines, the powerplant fitted to most Emirates A380s, after an uncontained engine failure forced an A380 to abort a takeoff.

    Sources indicate that aeroTime estimated that complying with the directive could cost up to $528,150 per affected engine, creating an immediate financial overhang whenever covered units come due for work. The reality is, however, that exact counts of affected engines across Emirates's fleet are not public, so it is vital to keep in mind that the per-engine estimate highlights unit-level exposure and does not necessarily translate into a confirmed fleetwide bill.

    Structural checks also interrupted availability earlier in the year, showing that airframe aging brings its own surprise bills. In June 2026, Airbus conducted inspections on 16 A380s, 15 of those being operated by Emirates, after cracks turned up in a key wing component, which resulted in unscheduled inspection work on high-utilization widebodies.

    Industry observers note that spending heavily on an airframe only pays off when the jet is generating revenue, though interestingly, nearly 30 Emirates A380s sat out of service at some point in 2026 due to cabin overhauls, routine maintenance, or temporary operational changes, as reported by Arabian Gulf Business Insight. Even with that downtime, Emirates expects roughly 110 A380s to be in active service by the end of 2026, showing how much capacity the airline can still field once aircraft cycle back onto the schedule instead of leaving the entire double-decker subfleet parked.

    Industry observers note that temporary schedule trims and flight reductions in 2026 show how quickly fleet availability ripples through Emirates's network from Dubai. When widebodies step off the line for maintenance, refurbishment, or operational adjustments, planners will need to trim frequencies or reshuffle aircraft assignments because stretching every remaining superjumbo indefinitely across long-haul sectors just doesn't work in this kind of scenario.

    Recent findings suggest that every parked or temporarily sidelined A380 carries an opportunity cost alongside direct upkeep, tying up high-capacity seats during peak travel windows when demand is high. Getting those grounded frames back into rotation and keeping the active core flying reliably is central to turning high fixed and maintenance spending into ticket revenue.

    It is clear today that the A380 is not something that the vast majority of airlines want, but Emirates still accepts the steep hourly burn, multi-billion-dollar cabin spending, and sudden technical bills. The reason for this is that Emirates President Tim Clark regards the Airbus A380 as "the most profitable asset in our fleet." Where other airlines have widely regarded the four-engine superjumbo as an oversized relic that is expensive to fill and costly to power, Emirates sees its high-capacity footprint as a core commercial engine when demand peaks on major trunk routes.

    Industry observers note that no aircraft right now in production matches the A380's passenger capacity in a single airframe, which explains why Emirates intends to fly the type until roughly 2041 despite persistent four-engine cost pressure. Replacing hundreds of double-decker seats at slot-constrained airports with smaller twin-engine widebodies would mean that Emirates has to add more frequencies or leave high-demand departures with fewer seats to sell during peak periods.

    Even so, keeping an aging four-engine type flying toward 2041 is not a free pass from economic friction, since fuel volatility and higher maintenance intensity continually test that profitability thesis. Emirates holds on to that massive revenue-generating capacity, but something naturally has to give. That being the high per-hour costs and long-horizon airframe support, which will continue to be the defining trade-off behind Emirates's willingness to pay for the A380.

    Sources indicate that whether the A380 can stay as a commercial winner for Emirates through the next decade is really dependent on how fuel prices behave after the 2026 Iran conflict shock and how quickly replacement widebody deliveries arrive. The higher-than-ever jet fuel costs hit four-engine economics harder than twin-engine competitors, while ongoing OEM delivery delays determine how long Emirates must lean on refurbished double-deckers to hold capacity across major trunk routes without losing market share at slot-constrained hubs.

    December 2026 offers an immediate checkpoint on that trajectory, as Emirates aims to have more than half of its 219-aircraft cabin retrofit program completed and roughly 110 A380s in active service by year-end. Meeting those targets, all while managing unscheduled engine and airframe checks, from turbine seal directives to structural inspections, will be what shows whether Emirates can keep its biggest revenue earner ahead of its rising upkeep as aircraft cycle through hangars.

    The question that many still have is how smoothly a replacement aircraft eventually arrives, which at the moment is considered to be the Boeing 777X, and how stubborn fuel and maintenance expenses prove over the coming years. Whatever the future holds, it ultimately will decide whether keeping the A380 flying until about 2041 stays an asset or turns into a heavier burden. For now, Emirates is betting that unmatched single-airframe scale outweighs higher per-hour and refurbishment costs, even as every shift in oil prices or delivery schedules tests the margin on that strategy.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, powerful storms bringing high winds and the potential for flooding could seriously disrupt commercial air travel in the U.S. during the single busiest week of the year.

    Forecasters are warning that storm systems will likely strike parts of the South, Mid-Atlantic, and Northeast, as well as Northern California and the Pacific Northwest. These regions are home to some of the nation’s busiest airports, through which millions of American travelers will pass this week en route to visit family and friends for Thanksgiving on Thursday.

    In the Northeast, the remnants of a weakened, disorganized system were still clearing out on Monday. A much stronger storm is expected to develop in the Gulf of Mexico between Monday and Tuesday, impact parts of the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic Wednesday, and slam into the New York metro area and New England on Thanksgiving Day.

    Industry observers note that according to an advisory from the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center, strong wind gusts up to 50 mph will be felt from the Carolinas to Maine. Flooding and beach erosion could be seen in coastal areas due to the already high tides.

    Recent findings suggest that WPC has initiated Key Messages for a Thanksgiving Coastal Storm that is expected to impact the U.S. East Coast. pic.twitter.com/pdQuU4U4yG.

    Americans traveling from, through, or to these areas should prepare for the possibility of flooded roads, damage from high winds, and power outages, the agency remarked.

    NYC Emergency Management noted Sunday that the storm could bring gusts of 40 to 45 mph and about one to two inches of rain to the city.

    Industry observers note that for Upcoming York and New England, the storm will be at its strongest Thursday evening. Parts of the Adirondacks and northern New England could see ice and snow mixed in with rain.

    It has been revealed that in California, Oregon, and Washington, residents still recovering from flooding last week could be hit again by rain and strong winds. A new system is expected to move in Tuesday and Wednesday; combined with the “king tides,” the storm could cause flooding up and down the West Coast.

    Industry observers note that the impact is expected to be most severe between Portland, Oregon, and San Francisco. San Francisco’s mayor remarked residents should take the forecasts seriously and consider not traveling for the holiday.

    The Sierra Nevada, meanwhile, will see fresh snow, meteorologists said.

    Over six million people are expected to fly within the U.S. this week for Thanksgiving. The surge is already underway, with many carriers adding flights to accommodate the increased traffic. American Airlines earlier this month projected its busiest Thanksgiving week since before the COVID-19 pandemic; that prediction could hold true for other U.S. airlines as well.

    AirlineGeeks will continue to monitor weather conditions and provide updates as the week progresses.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The real-world value of choosing the right credit cards for your everyday spending We frequently tout the incredible value you can get from top rewards credit cards — from bonus categories to welcome offers, lucrative benefits to monthly statement credits.

    But exactly how much value can you get from matching the right credit cards to your spending habits?

    Well, we recently set out to answer this very question.

    We challenged three American households with a simple question: Can you make the money you’re already spending work harder for you?

    The answer was a resounding yes.

    Mollie and Kevin were up first. The pair recently moved in together ahead of their wedding, and they’re working through how to combine their finances while also saving for their dream honeymoon to Thailand and Vietnam. Both had travel rewards cards before the challenge, but they weren’t coordinating their purchases.

    Plus, they were still using debit cards for some everyday expenses.

    In short, they had room for improvement in how they made the most of the cards in their wallets.

    They started by sitting down to map out their spending habits, which uncovered three primary categories being spread across multiple cards, without any rhyme or reason:.

    Plus, they had some major wedding expenses coming up, which gave them a great opportunity to snag a upcoming card with a lucrative welcome bonus.

    By coordinating their household spending, closing duplicate cards and opening a new one for the welcome offer, they’re now earning more from the same purchases they were already making.

    The remaining balance of the catering bill for their wedding alone hit the minimum spending required to earn the welcome offer, and when all was said and done, the couple took home 120,000 points — worth nearly $2,500 based on TPG’s most recent valuations.

    Recent findings suggest that next stop for Mollie and Kevin? Southeast Asia.

    Next, we meet Amy, a single mom of two daughters in Maryland. She’s been earning rewards on her favorite hotel cobranded card for years, using it for basically every purchase she could — from utilities to groceries to clothing. She’s racked up nearly 400,000 points in the process, which have come in handy as her daughters have begun traveling for dance competitions.

    It has been revealed that however, she was concerned her hotel loyalty meant she was sacrificing some value. Could she shift some of her spending to a new card to diversify her rewards?

    With back-to-school shopping and dance classes making up the bulk of her spending in the next month, she opted to add a latest card to her wallet that offered solid rewards on all purchases — along with some easy-to-use statement credits.

    And a large home repair bill accelerated her progress toward earning the welcome bonus — a great way to make the best of an unexpected expense.

    Industry observers note that she’s still keeping her old hotel card open, since it features a low annual fee, and she’ll still want to earn (and redeem) those points when it works. However, the rewards on her newly introduced card give her the newfound flexibility she didn’t have originally.

    “I really had tunnel vision with the hotel points,” she admitted. “I was leaving money on the table.".

    Our final household focuses on Denver, a travel enthusiast who was thrown a pair of major life curveballs last year when her grandfather passed away, and her mom lost her job (and thus her source of income). She moved back home to help, and travel (understandably) shifted to the back burner.

    Industry observers note that while Denver charged many purchases to her favorite travel rewards card, she had other purchases pulled straight from her bank account. She was also worried that putting everything on her credit card would encourage her to spend more. However, there was a key opportunity in her new role as a caretaker: focusing on everyday spending rather than travel rewards.

    Denver opted for a new cash-back credit card with bonuses at grocery stores, on streaming services and at gas stations. It even offered a one-time $300 cash-back bonus. These rewards can immediately help offset her household bills, like medication costs, be saved for an unexpected expense, or even go toward a future getaway with her family.

    She’s continuing to pay her statement balance in full and on time, so it’s not about spending more; it’s about smarter spending based on her current situation.

    After just a month, Denver is tracking toward nearly $1,500 in cash-back rewards in the first year — just by being more intentional with her everyday spending.

    One of the most common questions we get here at TPG is, “What’s the best credit card for me?” And there’s a simple answer: “It depends.”.

    It has been revealed that everyone’s situation is unique, so there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to maximizing your everyday spending. And these three households demonstrate that exact phenomenon.

    It has been revealed that one went with a new travel card to maximize their wedding purchases. Another opted for a flexible rewards card to diversify her earnings. And the third focused on a cash-back card to support her family’s bottom line.

    All of them are now getting even more value from the purchases they were already making.

    This is the power of matching the cards in your wallet to your daily spending — while keeping a keen eye on earning the rewards that work best for you.

    It has been revealed that don’t miss out on the chance to make your everyday purchases work harder for you. Analyze where you’re spending your money today, so you can unlock even more value tomorrow.

The aircraft had pitched up to climb away when the underside of its rear fuselage scraped the runway, sending sparks flying on a live broadcast from Airline Videos.

    In a recent development, originating from Boston (BOS), tail number N2193J was attempting to land on Runway 25L at 11:44 PM local time when the crew initiated the ill-fated go-around. Following the contact, the pilots climbed out safely, repositioned for a second approach to Runway 25L, and landed without further incident roughly 16 minutes later at 12:01 AM.

    While the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) logged a preliminary incident report noting the go-around tail strike, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has not yet listed a formal investigation while the extent of the physical damage is assessed. The plane involved is a 2-year-old Airbus A321-271NX named 'StateMint Piece,' which was delivered to JetBlue in December 2024. Its scheduled return leg as Flight B6524 to Fresh York-JFK (JFK) at 2:30 PM today was canceled.

    In a recent development, the last tail strike by a JetBlue-operated aircraft occurred in February at San Francisco International Airport (SFO). That A321neo, tail N2188J, was also flying into the West Coast from Boston. Operating as Flight B62233, it struck its tail on Runway 28L at SFO during landing. According to the NTSB final report via AeroCorner, the jet bounced upon touchdown, and the first officer pulled the sidestick fully aft while applying go-around power, causing substantial damage to the lower fuselage.

    The Aviation Safety Network reports on another tail strike by a plane flown by JetBlue in 2022. That Airbus A320, tail N760JB, was damaged during takeoff out of Hayden, Colorado, due to confusion with local general aviation traffic and pilot error. While attempting to coordinate with a Beechcraft B300 King Air that was inbound, the crew performed a rapid departure and rotated 24 knots under speed while also striking the tail of the jet.

    Fortunately, in all three instances of recent tail strike mishaps for JetBlue air crews, no injuries were reported aboard any of the planes. While formal findings are still pending from Sunday night's incident, the video showing a shower of sparks during the late-night go-around means that there will be repairs to paint, scraped-off rivets, and potentially failed fuselage panels. • Lower fuselage protrusions, like heated drain masts and VHF/transponder antennas, may have also been sheared off or crushed.

    In a recent development, following the accident at SFO, tail N2188J suffered what the NTSB described as substantial damage. Post-flight inspections documented significant scraping and abrasion across the lower aft skin, along with damage to a pitot tube. As the jet bounced twice before the first officer pulled full aft sidestick, the impact required major repairs to restore the lower fuselage skin and support structure before the aircraft could return to service.

    It has been revealed that similarly, tail N760JB saw substantial abrasion damage across multiple fuselage frames, according to NTSB post-mishap inspections. Notably, the crew did not initially realize they had struck the tail until air traffic control alerted them at 31,000 feet (9,448.8 meters), prompting an immediate diversion to Denver. Since the tail-strike damage may have compromised pressurized sections of the rear fuselage, the aircraft cannot safely fly at high altitude and must be repaired on-site or flown at low altitude to a maintenance base.

    It has been revealed that for tail N2193J, the process is well underway to find the damage and correct it so that the plane can return to service safely. Immediately after landing, maintenance crews would have pulled the Cockpit Voice Recorder and Flight Data Recorder. The FAA and NTSB will analyze exact pitch angles, airspeed, and stick inputs at the critical phase of flight when the mishap occurred.

    If the damage is considered to be superficial within the allowable limits for skin abrasion set by Airbus, mechanics at LAX can install an aerodynamic 'scab patch,' or doubler. If the inspection finds substantial damage, then engineers will need to be involved to develop a custom repair scheme.

    Should that be necessary, the plane will fly under 10,000 feet (3,048 meters) per a 'ferry permit' to make its way to a proper maintenance, repair, and overhaul depot that can handle the scope of work. As for the pilots, the typical procedure is focused on identifying safety failures and retraining rather than punishment. That is provided that the accident was not a result of misconduct.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Populism, for all of its faults, can be a powerful force in politics when it is rising.
    • It has been revealed that as I’ve noted before, the very nature of populism is that it has to redefine The People to include something less than all the people when it inevitably encounters the reality that its premises are not universally shared.
    • Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    Populism, for all of its faults, can be a powerful force in politics when it is rising. While populist agendas can come in many different varieties, they are all propelled by a broad sense that the people — or more properly, The People — are being held back by some elite force, whether that be Major Business or an insular political establishment or something darker. If only we can overcome the enemy, we are told, we will sweep to victory on the broad, sunny uplands.

    It has been revealed that as I’ve noted before, the very nature of populism is that it has to redefine The People to include something less than all the people when it inevitably encounters the reality that its premises are not universally shared. And so it goes from there, because populism always sooner or later must decide to cling to its narratives when forced to choose between them and empirical reality:.

    Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    On “Populism Isn’t Built for Setbacks”.

    House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, states banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the problem could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, states banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the problem could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    It has been revealed that “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” stated Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks glitch with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner noted he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the fresh Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    Recent findings suggest that “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Folding newly introduced language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    According to recent reports, colorado Rep. Jason Crow remarked moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    “I want to pursue a parallel track,” mentioned Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly noted the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    Sources indicate that “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he noted at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Recent findings suggest that some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    It has been revealed that rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., noted she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she mentioned of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    Recent findings suggest that that measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    Sources indicate that “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    It has been revealed that it’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a upcoming stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    “My district, Latest York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and indicates right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that while momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    Industry observers note that as they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    It has been revealed that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he stated. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley noted that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    #168479. Industry News: A Japanese WWII Bomber & A Crashed Continental Boeing 727: The Unlikely Wrecks Hidden In A Pacific Jungle

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1555 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: A Japanese WWII Bomber & A Crashed Continental Boeing 727: The Unlikely Wrecks Hidden In A Pacific Jungle

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, in October and November 2026, I visited the island of Yap in the eastern Pacific.
    • Industry observers note that just next to the old, overgrown Japanese airfield is the functioning Yap International Airport.
    • Since then, the forest has regrown, and visitors can see what remains of a Japanese Second World War bomber and a Continental Boeing 727 lying side-by-side in the jungle as strange bedfellows.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, in October and November 2026, I visited the island of Yap in the eastern Pacific. There, I explored an old Japanese Second World War airfield that had been bombed by the United States during the Second World War. Following the war, the jungle regrew and claimed the various abandoned Japanese aircraft wrecks.

    Industry observers note that just next to the old, overgrown Japanese airfield is the functioning Yap International Airport. In 1980, Continental Airlines (Air Micronesia) Boeing 727 operating as Flight 614 crashed while landing. The wreck burned out, although all passengers survived. It came to rest just next to a Mitsubishi G4M 'Betty' bomber at the old Japanese airfield.

    Since then, the forest has regrown, and visitors can see what remains of a Japanese Second World War bomber and a Continental Boeing 727 lying side-by-side in the jungle as strange bedfellows. The local volunteer pilot, Amos Collins, highlighted me the two wrecks that I had failed to find by myself.

    Today, Yap is one of the islands that make up the independent nation of the Federated States of Micronesia. During the Second World War, it was controlled by Japan under the League of Nations South Seas Mandate. These were islands that Japan had wrestled control of from Germany in the First World War.

    According to recent reports, the island of Chuuk (Truk) became a major Japanese naval base, while others were heavily defended as strong points to protect the Japanese home islands. Yap was only lightly defended, being far behind the island chains deeper into the Pacific, and it wasn't until later in the Pacific War that Japan hurriedly moved to fortify the island.

    The ruins of Japanese Second World War aircraft, guns, and bunkers can be found across the island. I spent days seeking out and exploring them. According to a modern report by the United States Navy, in May 1944, the Japanese commander of the 22nd Air Flotilla at Chuuk issued orders for the 2nd Attack Force and other air groups to be stationed on Yap.

    Industry observers note that US military sorties later reported 24 Japanese fighter aircraft, six dive bombers, two medium bombers, and six night fighters on Yap. These later took part in counterattacking US efforts to bombard the Mariana Islands (such as Guam). The US Navy drew up a proposal to invade the island as it did with others. However, it soon abandoned the idea in favor of bombing, neutralizing, and bypassing it.

    Today, visitors can see the remains of many Japanese military aircraft destroyed on the ground at the airfield next to large bomb craters. Some of these wrecks are marked, others are not marked, or the signs have since disappeared. You should note that this is private property and visitors are expected to ask residents permission to explore them.

    I found around seven Japanese aircraft, or what remained of them. Here and there on the island, visitors can see the remains of US Vought F4U Corsair fighter planes and propellers of B-24 bombers that came down on the island. I mostly found the Corsair engines and B-24 propellers.

    Sources indicate that however, one of the most eye-catching wrecks is that of a Mitsubishi G4M medium bomber/torpedo bomber. Japan built a total of 2,435 of these twin-engined, seven-crew bombers. Presumably, this wreck is one of the two medium bombers US reconnaissance identified.

    It has been revealed that the wreck is located here on Google Maps, around a third of the way down the airstrip (now functioning as a potholed village road). It was the only Japanese wreck I found on the island that has its own dedicated information plaque. The plaque is so overgrown by algae that it's hard to make anything out. Most information plaques are for US military remains on the island.

    Continental Airlines established much of the infrastructure to provide scheduled air services to the Micronesian islands, which were then managed by the United States under the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. Essentially, the US took over the Japanese South Seas Mandate by another name. Continental set up its Air Micronesia brand to serve the islands.

    Eventually, this was all inherited by United Airlines following the merger. In November 1980, an Air Micronesia Boeing 727-92C (registered N18479) departed Saipan bound for Palau with island hopping stopovers in Guam and Yap. At 9:52 AM the aircraft touched down at Yap 13 feet short of runway 07. The Aviation Safety Network writes that:.

    "The right main landing gear immediately separated from the aircraft. The aircraft gradually veered off the runway and came to rest in the jungle about 1,700 feet beyond the initial touchdown.".

    The probable cause is given as the captain prematurely reducing thrust in combination with flying a shallow approach slope angle to an improper touchdown aim point. All 73 occupants were evacuated within around a minute of the aircraft coming to rest. Today, the heavily forested nature of the landscape makes it difficult to understand how the aircraft could have skidded without breaking up.

    According to recent reports, I was shown the Boeing 727 and its neighboring Japanese Betty bomber wreck by the volunteer pilot, Amos Collins, who flies for Pacific Missionary Aviation. Having made friends with Amos and being an aviation journalist, he invited me on the flight and then demonstrated me the wrecks. PMA is a hybrid charity airline operating in Micronesia.

    When we visited the bomber and 727, we had just gotten back from a supply flight to the outer Yap island of Ulithi on a Super King Air 200. The Boeing 727 caught fire after coming to a rest.

    It has been revealed that collins told me that the fire truck from neighboring Yap International Airport responded, only to find on site that the truck lacked any water. The stricken 727 subsequently burned down completely. He stated that the incident remains a joke among the Yap Airport fire crews today. The main section of the aircraft remaining is the tail, including one of its air intakes for the tail-mounted engine.

    Industry observers note that collins is the father of five, and he noted his children enjoy crawling through and using the air intake as a playground slide. I thought of climbing through it myself but decided against the idea. While it is difficult to make out in the photographs I took, the Boeing 727 and Betty bomber are literally a stone's throw from each other. A few feet (meters) more of skidding the 727 would have destroyed the Betty wreck.

    According to recent reports, only a minority of both aircraft exist today. The Mitsubishi G4M's cockpit is perhaps the best preserved. It still has the two pilots' seats and what is left of the controls. The control panel remains well-preserved, as does the aluminum frame. All rubber or other materials have since disappeared. The tail section is also relatively well-preserved, as is at least one propeller.

    It would seem that propellers have been removed from a number of sites over the years by the locals. Some sites do retain their propellers, but there are also very clearly some propellers on display at residents' homes, and two are on display at PMA's hangar. Regarding PMA's propellers, Collins told me they were from a B-24 and B-29 bomber. I don't know where they came from.

    Air Micronesia (Continental) Boeing 727.

    Sometimes just tails, sometimes relatively complete.

    As stated, only the Boeing 727's tail remains in place today. This is well-preserved, although the rest of the aircraft appears to have been destroyed or removed. Some salvageable components and materials were stripped over the decades, but the first consumed much of the forward and mid-fuselage. Various bits of debris can be found scattered throughout the surrounding jungle, but the tail is the main attraction.

    Recent findings suggest that the story of warplanes on Yap is not over, and a newly introduced chapter may yet be written. The United States retains responsibility for defending the islands; in practice, this also means the US has exclusive military basing rights. In a period of Great Power Competition with China, the US is moving to expand the airport infrastructure and defenses of the islands as part of the Second Island Chain.

    Congress has approved funds to significantly expand Yap International Airport as part of the Air Force's Agile Combat Employment doctrine to disperse aircraft from Guam's Andersen Air Force Base in the event of a high-end conflict. When I was there, ground on the project was not yet broken, and heavy machinery had yet to arrive.

    According to recent reports, work on Palau's Peleliu Airfield is in full swing. This raises the prospect that in a future high-end conflict, F-35 fighter jets, KC-46A tankers, and other modern US military aircraft could find themselves destroyed on the ground next to Japanese bombers and fighters long-lost in the jungle.

    Recent findings suggest that I asked Collins if he was concerned about the US preparing his remote island for war; he answered no. I asked if that was because he wasn't concerned, or if it was because he was committed to the island and there was nothing he could do with great power politics happening around them. If it's better to accept and get on with life. He said the latter.

    #168478. At the Races: The upcoming Trump Democrats

    📖 Baca

    At the Races: The upcoming Trump Democrats

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    According to recent reports, “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    It has been revealed that andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    Sources indicate that “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” remarked Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    It has been revealed that “I respect them,” he mentioned. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Sources indicate that peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Industry observers note that leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    It has been revealed that A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    Recent findings suggest that #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, launched his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he intends to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    It has been revealed that they’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    Recent findings suggest that RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    Recent findings suggest that thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Industry observers note that battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    In a recent development, #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    Industry observers note that new leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    Sources indicate that remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    Sources indicate that tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: Upcoming York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    According to recent reports, west Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    It has been revealed that the last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    In a recent development, monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly stated he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    • In a recent development, america’s leading natural gas competitor is on track to become its biggest customer.
    • In a recent development, doha’s ventures are adding up.
    • Natalie Ecanow is a research analyst for the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies.

    In a recent development, america’s leading natural gas competitor is on track to become its biggest customer. With traffic down through the Strait of Hormuz, Qatar is betting on U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG). The state’s energy organization, QatarEnergy, signed two purchase agreements for American LNG in late October and is reportedly in talks with U.S. supplier Venture Global for a third. There may yet be more deals coming down the pike, including one with Houston-based NextDecade. QatarEnergy already owns 70 percent of Golden Pass LNG, a joint venture with ExxonMobil that shipped its first cargo out of Sabine Pass, Texas, in April.

    In a recent development, doha’s ventures are adding up. So much so that, according to an early November Financial Times report, Qatar may become “the biggest U.S. LNG buyer” by 2033. This presents the United States with opportunities to affirm market leadership and drive a wedge between Doha and Tehran.

    Natalie Ecanow is a research analyst for the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies. Her work focuses on the Middle East.

    On “How Washington Could Exploit Qatar’s LNG Shopping Spree”.

    United Airlines’ Most Frequent Boeing 777-200 Flights In 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Boeing 777-200 entered service in 1994 and was primarily aimed at US domestic airlines; the 777-200ER followed in 1997 with more of an international focus.
    • In a recent development, here is what to know about where United Airlines is flying its Boeing 777-200/ER fleet in 2026, according to data provided by Cirium, a data analytics company.
    • In a recent development, united Airlines operates a fleet of 74 Boeing 777-200/ER airliners, of which Planespotters.net lists 61 as active and 13 as parked.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Boeing 777-200 entered service in 1994 and was primarily aimed at US domestic airlines; the 777-200ER followed in 1997 with more of an international focus. The 777-200ER extends the range from around 5,240 nautical miles to 7,065 nautical miles (depending on mission profile). These are workhorses for United's transatlantic routes, as well as some inter-hub routes, routes to Hawaii, and select destinations in East Asia. The type is aging, with older examples struggling with fuel efficiency compared with modern aircraft, although as paid-off aircraft, they also offer much lower capital expenses for United.

    In a recent development, here is what to know about where United Airlines is flying its Boeing 777-200/ER fleet in 2026, according to data provided by Cirium, a data analytics company. The flight data below is for the full 2026 calendar year and includes both the 777-200 and the 777-200ER, as Cirium lacks distinct aircraft codes for the sub-variants. The data is also for the full year, even if the 777s were replaced with other aircraft partway through the year on the routes.

    In a recent development, united Airlines operates a fleet of 74 Boeing 777-200/ER airliners, of which Planespotters.net lists 61 as active and 13 as parked. The overall age of the fleet is rapidly aging and is now 27.5 years old. These include 19 Boeing 777-200s, with the remainder being 777-200ERs. United is the launch customer and the largest operator of the 777-200, with the fleet being configured for domestic routes. The 777-200ER includes four examples with domestic configurations. The remainder of the 777-200ER is configured for international operations.

    According to Planespotters.net, United has not divested any of its 777-200/ERs since 2005, after eight examples had been transferred to Indian and Brazilian operators. The oldest example in United's service is registered N777UA and was delivered in 1995, making it 31.5 years old. The youngest member of the family is registered as N27015 and was delivered in 2010. It is now around 26.7 years old.

    In a recent development, cirium's data highlights United is operating the 777-200/ER from its six main hubs: San Francisco (12,591 route-pair flights), Newark (6,635), Houston (5,549), Washington Dulles (4,900), Denver (3,059), and Chicago O'Hare (1,165). Adding these directly would result in double counting of 1,759 flights due to flights between the hubs. For the full year, United is expected to operate a total of 32,140 flights with the aircraft carrying a total of 9.6 million seats.

    Sources indicate that chicago O'Hare sees the fewest flights with United's Boeing 777-200/ERs. Its most frequent pairings (outbound and inbound) are to its other hubs, including 373 flights on the San Francisco pairing (1,604 nautical miles), 309 flights on the Los Angeles pairing (1,517 nautical miles), and 236 flights on the Denver pairing (772 nautical miles). The year is also seeing 174 flights from Chicago to Mexico's Cancun (1,255 nautical miles).

    Denver is to see 3,059 United 777-200 family flights carrying 1.1 million seats. Its leading routes by distance and frequency are to Hawaii, including Honolulu (1,226 flights at 2,929 nautical miles), Maui (744 flights at 2,872 nautical miles), and Kona (238 flights at 2,894 nautical miles). That is a total of 2,248 flights on Denver's Hawaii pairings and 73% of the airports' total United 777-200/ER operations.

    Most frequent United 777-200/ER pairings.

    Washington Dulles - London Heathrow.

    San Francisco - London Heathrow.

    Industry observers note that other routes include Chicago O'Hare, already mentioned above (236 flights), Houston (225 flights), Cancun (174), as well as a limited number of flights to San Francisco, Orlando, and Washington Dulles. In other words, most of United's non-Hawaii paired 777-200/ER flights from Denver are to its other major hubs in the continental United States.

    According to recent reports, washington Dulles has 4,900 United 777-200/ER operations, with the bulk of these being transatlantic flights to Western Europe. Dulles' most frequent pairing is with London Heathrow at 996 flights, followed by Germany's Frankfurt (744 flights). The next most common pairing is transpacific to Tokyo Haneda, with 728 flights. After that Japanese route, it's back to Europe with the pairings to Paris (656 flights), Lisbon (557 flights), and Rome Fiumicino (492 flights).

    Other European pairings include Athens (168), Brussels (126), Barcelona (32), and Zurich (18). Domestic routes are to San Francisco (193 flights) and Los Angeles (136 flights). Most European routes from Dulles average between 3,000 and 4,000 nautical miles, although the route to Athens is considerably longer, reaching 4,492 nautical miles. United Airlines dominates Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), accounting for roughly 66% to 70% of passenger traffic.

    From Dulles, United connects the US capital with various intercontinental destinations in Europe, Asia, and even Africa. Somewhat surprisingly, given the US's strong demographic and cultural connections with South America, the only route to that continent operated by United is to São Paulo with Boeing 767-400ERs. Avianca also operates flights between Bogotá and Washington Dulles. The lack of flights is because airlines concentrate US–South America hubs in southern and coastal gateways (Miami, Houston) with stronger passenger demand.

    Recent findings suggest that in Houston, George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) is dominated by United Airlines, while William P. Hobby Airport (HOU) is dominated by Southwest Airlines. At IAH, United boasts around 74.1% of the passenger market share, perhaps more now that Spirit has collapsed. Spirit had around 5% of the market share. From Houston, the most frequent 777-200/ER route is to London Heathrow, whose pairing is seeing 1,397 flights in 2026.

    Houston is also a significant gateway to South America, with the next busiest pairing being with Buenos Aires (942 flights). The only other South American destination is Chile's Santiago, with 209 flights. These are United's main routes to South America, meaning they aren't used very heavily in that direction. There are no frequent United 777-200/ER routes to Mexico, the Caribbean, or Central America. This is partly due to many of these destinations being within range of narrowbody aircraft. For example, United operates seven daily A320-family flights between Houston and Mexico City.

    The third-busiest pairing is with United's West Coast hub of San Francisco (681 flights), with another 225 flights on the Houston-Denver route and 52 flights on the Houston-Newark route. The other regular routes are transatlantic routes to Germany, with the Frankfurt pairing getting 730 flights in 2026 and Munich getting 580. Munich is the longest route at an average distance of 4,708 nautical miles, followed by Frankfurt, Buenos Aires, London Heathrow, and Santiago — all of which are above 4,000 nautical miles.

    The airport that hosts the second-most United 777-200/ER flights is Newark Liberty, with 6,635 operations. United Airlines holds roughly 60% to 68% of passenger market share at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), making it by far the airport's dominant carrier and largest hub. It is from Newark that United connects the New York region with much of the world, including many transatlantic destinations in Europe.

    Sources indicate that even so, the single busiest city pairing is with San Francisco, with 1,314 flights, while the second-busiest transcontinental pairing is with Los Angeles, with 710 flights. Otherwise, transatlantic routes dominate the list and include Paris (863 flights), Dublin (728 flights), Milan (582 flights), London Heathrow (413 flights), Amsterdam (284 flights), Munich (205 flights), Barcelona (184 flights), and Rome (139 flights).

    It has been revealed that other notable city pairings include Tokyo Haneda (593 flights) and São Paulo, Brazil (526 flights). The Tokyo route is notable for being one of the longest routes United is assigning its 777-200ERs, at an average distance of 5,877 nautical miles. At the moment, United is operating a daily flight to Tokyo Haneda using its 787-9s, suggesting the 777-200ERs have been pulled off the route. United is also operating 787-9s on the twin Newark-Tokyo Narita route.

    Recent findings suggest that san Francisco is by far the busiest hub for United's fleet of 777-200/ERs in 2026, with a total of 12,591 operations. Being located on the West Coast, San Francisco also sees the largest range of destinations, with flights to Asia, Australia, Fresh Zealand, Europe, and domestic destinations within the United States. The busiest pairing is the one mentioned above with Newark Liberty (1,314 flights).

    European routes include Frankfurt (1,077 flights), London Heathrow (744 flights), Paris (656 flights), Munich (716 flights), Rome (410 flights), Barcelona (266 flights), Zurich (262 flights), and Amsterdam (238 flights). Routes to East Asia are Tokyo Haneda (730), Beijing (728), Osaka (714), Taipei (690), Seoul (273), and Tokyo Narita (239). Already mentioned above are other hub pairings with Houston, Chicago, and Washington.

    San Francisco, along with Denver, is a major hub for flights to Hawaii's Honolulu (794). San Francisco is also the only hub where United's 777-200/ERs are flying to Australia (Brisbane with 524 flights and Sydney with 296 flights) and Latest Zealand (Auckland with 490 flights). The Sydney route is the longest one of all for United's 777-200ERs with an average distance of 6,447 nautical miles followed by Brisbane at 6,140 nautical miles. New Zealand is a bit closer at 5,665 nautical miles.

    In a recent development, an Alaska Airlines flight was delayed by hours after masked ICE agents stormed the jet bridge of a departing flight to arrest a Mexican national who allegedly had a work permit had overstayed his visa (you know, “the worst of the worst”). This ended up turning into a huge jet bridge melee, leading to additional arrests, as ICE claims that someone hurled hot coffee at the officers.

    It has been revealed that in the end, the flight was delayed by hours, as the crew was no longer fit to fly, and the Port of Seattle is outraged. This is quite the story, as flagged by PYOK.

    This incident happened on the morning of Saturday, November 21, 2026, and involves Alaska Airlines flight AS1306, scheduled to operate from Seattle (SEA) to Los Angeles (LAX).

    This was first reported by a passenger on the flight, who explained that “ICE agents just arrested multiple people at SeaTac Airport inside the jet bridge as we were all boarding,” and went on to explain that they were “deplaning because the crew is being replaced due to poor morale.”.

    ICE agents just arrested multiple people at SeaTac Airport inside the jet bridge as we were all boarding. Now deplaning because the crew is being replaced due to poor morale @CNN @nytimes @seattletimes.

    Video taken from the jet bridge shows masked ICE agents trying to arrest people on the jet bridge.

    It has been revealed that masked ICE agents detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers were boarding a flight. Alaska Airlines stated ICE officers gave them no advance notice of the operation. pic.twitter.com/r44WPTvGdv.

    Recent findings suggest that as a result of this incident, the Alaska flight ended up being delayed by hours. It was initially supposed to depart at 8:10AM and arrive at 11:01AM, but instead, departed at 11:03AM and arrived at 1:36PM.

    Here’s how ICE explained its actions:.

    On November 21, 2026, at approximately 8:05 a.m. PST, ICE officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an illegal alien from Mexico who overstayed his visa in violation of our nation’s laws.

    During the arrest other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers—a federal crime and a felony. One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers. Other passengers began obstructing federal officers.

    According to recent reports, the individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay. She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

    It has been revealed that assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony. Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the fullest extent of the law.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that an Alaska Airlines Boeing 737-800 has been temporarily grounded in New York after colliding with a catering vehicle ahead of a flight to San Francisco International (SFO).
    • A video uploaded to social media by one of the passengers demonstrated the aftermath of the collision, which saw the wing of the 737 come into contact with a truck.
    • In a recent development, alaska Airlines flight AS41 is a daily scheduled service from New York to San Francisco.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that an Alaska Airlines Boeing 737-800 has been temporarily grounded in New York after colliding with a catering vehicle ahead of a flight to San Francisco International (SFO). The jet, which bears the registration N548AS, was set to depart from John F Kennedy Airport (JFK) on Monday evening as Alaska Airlines flight AS41.

    A video uploaded to social media by one of the passengers demonstrated the aftermath of the collision, which saw the wing of the 737 come into contact with a truck. Such was the extent of the damage that the flight ended up having to be canceled. A similar incident also befell a United Airlines Airbus A320 this year, which resulted in the jet being taken out of service for good. Let's examine Monday's events.

    In a recent development, alaska Airlines flight AS41 is a daily scheduled service from New York to San Francisco. It is one of the carrier's longest transcontinental flights, with a block time of six hours and 41 minutes between its planned departure from JFK at 5:25 PM and its scheduled arrival into the Bay Area at 9:06 PM (all times local). The iteration of this flight on Monday, November 23, however, ended up having to be canceled.

    In a recent development, this, as seen in the clip above, was due to the jet having been hit by a catering truck on the ground at JFK ahead of its departure. The Aviation Safety Network reported that "the ventral strake of the left-hand split scimitar winglet" bore the brunt of the damage, which was severe enough to take the jet out of service. Passengers were then told that the damaged Boeing 737 would return to the gate to deplane.

    Simple Flying has reached out to Alaska Airlines for further information on this incident. We will patch our coverage upon receiving a statement from the carrier.

    Recent findings suggest that winglets play an vital role in reducing drag and improving fuel efficiency, but they are also exposed to potential damage during ground operations, particularly when aircraft are moving around busy airport aprons. Even minimal damage can require inspections and repairs before an aircraft is cleared to fly again. Although the damage was enough to cancel the flight, the aircraft's eventual return to service will depend on the extent of the damage and the repairs required.

    Recent findings suggest that for the passengers impacted by Monday evening's cancelation of flight AS41, Alaska Airlines appears to have scheduled an extra flight to San Francisco on Tuesday morning, numbered AS9230, which is scheduled to depart JFK at 9:00 AM. The carrier schedules up to four flights a day between New York JFK and San Francisco, with departures spread throughout the day to optimize connectivity.

    In a recent development, according to fleet data from ch-aviation, N548AS is one of 59 examples of the Boeing 737-800 that Alaska Airlines currently has at its disposal. These narrowbody twinjets are 18.7 years old on average, although N548AS is one of the more senior examples, having first flown 21.45 years ago. It was delivered to Alaska Airlines on July 1, 2005, and it currently seats 161 passengers across two classes.

    Recent findings suggest that it remains to be seen exactly how badly N548AS has been damaged as a result of its ground collision on Monday evening. However, such incidents can end up being more terminal for older aircraft, such as N470UA, a United Airlines Airbus A320-200 that was hit by a truck in Washington in May 2026.

    Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

    According to recent reports, the narrowbody twinjet was already more than 25 years old at the time, having first flown in 2001, and the extent of the damage meant it made more economic sense to scrap the aircraft than repair it for a reentry into service. The plane remained on the ground at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) for several months before, as Planespotters.net notes, being broken up in October.

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that listen closely, and you will notice that Ben Sasse uses the word “glorious” often.
    • This historian by training, turnaround specialist by trade, former senator by a felt obligation, is the rare conservative undeterred by fatalism, even — especially — when staring it in the face.

    Industry observers note that listen closely, and you will notice that Ben Sasse uses the word “glorious” often. He uses it for the everyday goodness of Americans, the architecture of limited government they inherited, and now for his own rendezvous with God. Death by metastatic pancreatic cancer, Sasse indicates, is “what I need.”.

    This historian by training, turnaround specialist by trade, former senator by a felt obligation, is the rare conservative undeterred by fatalism, even — especially — when staring it in the face. In wisdom tucked into a footnote in his second book, Sasse doesn’t deny that the world is a “broken place always at risk of spinning out of control.” It’s just that he finds this unruliness quieting in a way, and responds with “profound gratitude for the gifts we’ve received and consequently aims to conserve or preserve those blessings.”.

    John R. Puri is the Thomas L. Rhodes Fellow at National Review.
